Rheovision software automates and controls test parameters. The footprint is 1' x 1' x 2', described by Brookfield as compact enough for site-to-site mobility.

sections.title: Pressure and Temperature Control
sections.tabSummary: Why boil-off is the problem this design addresses
body: Why boil-off is the problem this design addresses.

A volatile fluid tested at ambient pressure and elevated temperature can boil off before or during measurement, changing its composition and invalidating the result. PVS Rheometer's coaxial cylinder chamber operates under pressure specifically to prevent that — up to 1000 psi, across a temperature range of -40°C to +260°C, which Brookfield states makes it suitable for elevated or reduced temperature testing where boil-off would otherwise be an issue.

An RTD sensor mounted on the inner cylinder surface measures sample temperature directly at the point of shear, rather than inferring it from the chamber wall or an external probe. A safety relief valve is fitted as standard, addressing the operational risk of running a sealed chamber under both pressure and temperature extremes.

cards.title: Accurate measurement at very low shear rates
Coverage into higher shear conditions on the same instrument

paragraphs: Many process conditions — down-hole drilling, slow blending, reactor flow — happen at shear rates well below what a standard rotational instrument resolves accurately. PVS Rheometer measures down to 0.2 sec⁻¹ for low shear rate viscosity (LSRV) work, extending the usable range into conditions that matter directly for in-process simulation.

At the other end, the outer cylinder rotates at shear rates up to 1700 sec⁻¹, with a stationary spindle inside, giving the instrument range across both slow and fast shear conditions on the same coaxial cylinder geometry. Where the fluid itself is low-viscosity and the standard geometry doesn't provide enough measurement sensitivity, the optional triple annulus geometry increases sensitivity specifically for that case.

body: Why cone/plate and concentric cylinder on the same platform matters.

Different materials and test protocols call for different rheometer geometries — cone/plate suits certain viscosity ranges and sample volumes, concentric cylinder suits others. Buying separate instruments for each geometry means separate footprints, separate calibration routines, and separate operator training. RSO Rheometer supports both configurations on the same instrument, described by Brookfield as instrument flexibility suited to a wide range of material testing applications.

A quick connect coupling system attaches spindles without a lengthy fitting process, and automatic gap setting handles the spindle-to-plate distance that cone/plate geometry depends on for accurate shear rate calculation — a step that's traditionally manual and operator-sensitive on other instruments. Spindle barcode recognition identifies which geometry and spindle configuration is fitted automatically, reducing the chance of a test running against the wrong configuration data.

body: Why 200 Nm matters against a standard motor.

Testing high-viscosity or highly structured materials — pastes, gels, filled compounds — requires enough torque to actually shear the sample without the motor stalling or the measurement losing accuracy at the top of its range. RSX Coaxial Cylinder's 200 Nm motor is described by Brookfield specifically as an increase over a standard motor, aimed at testing the toughest samples for comprehensive analysis across a wide range of materials.

body: Why having both modes on one instrument matters.

Some rheological questions are best answered by fixing the shear rate and observing how stress responds; others need the reverse — fixing shear stress and observing the resulting shear rate, particularly around yield behavior. RSX Cone Plate runs both: controlled shear rate (rpm) and controlled shear stress (torque), named explicitly as distinct operating modes rather than one general controlled-shear description.

That distinction matters for method design. A test protocol built around controlled stress — common for yield stress work — and one built around controlled rate — common for standard flow curve generation — can both run on the same instrument without switching hardware, only the operating mode.

sections.title: Why Vane and Cross-Hatch Geometry
sections.tabSummary: The slippage problem this design solves
body: The slippage problem this design solves.

Standard cone/plate or smooth cylinder geometry works because the sample shears cleanly against the measuring surface. Pastes, slurries, and soft solids often don't behave that way — instead of shearing internally, the material slips at the surface of a smooth spindle or plate, which corrupts the measurement without necessarily looking wrong to the operator.

RSX SST addresses that specifically with vane and cross-hatch spindle geometries, described by Brookfield as used specifically to minimize slippage in soft-solid and paste-like samples. A vane geometry effectively traps material between its blades so the sample shears against itself rather than against a smooth surface; cross-hatch geometry provides a textured surface with the same intent.

paragraphs: Soft solids raise questions a simple viscosity number doesn't answer — how much a material deforms under sustained load before recovering or failing (creep), the stress at which it starts to flow at all (yield stress), and how its viscosity changes as shear conditions vary. RSX SST names all three as core capabilities rather than treating one as primary and the others as secondary.

Both controlled shear rate and controlled shear stress modes support these measurements, since yield stress testing in particular is often better approached through controlled stress ramps than fixed-rate testing. Running all three measurement types on the vane or cross-hatch geometry means the same sample and the same instrument setup can answer multiple questions about a soft solid's behavior without switching hardware between tests.
